summaries.example: Imagine a manager fires Maya because she is a girl, even though the manager does not fire boys in the same situation. Maya is put at a disadvantage because of a trait she has. Philosophers use cases like this to ask what makes something discrimination.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what discrimination is and why it may be wrong. A useful starting idea is that discrimination happens when a person is put at a disadvantage because of a trait, such as age, religion, sex, disability, or race. Philosophers debate whether the disadvantage must be compared with how other people are treated, or whether it is enough that the person would have done better without that trait. They also ask whether the trait must be part of someone’s reason, or whether it can cause the bad result without anyone noticing it. A rule about height, for example, might hurt one group more than another even if the rule never mentions that group. Finally, philosophers disagree about the wrongness of discrimination. It may cause harm, show disrespect, express a hurtful social message, or involve more than one of these problems. The word can describe an action without automatically proving that the action is morally wrong, although it often makes people suspect wrongdoing.
key_ideas: A basic definition says discrimination disadvantages someone because of a trait.
Philosophers disagree about what counts as a disadvantage and how the trait must be connected to it.
A rule can be unfair even when the person making the rule does not think about the trait directly.
Some philosophers explain wrongness through harm, disrespect, social messages, or several of these together.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make choices about jobs, homes, schools, services, and friendships. Understanding discrimination helps us ask careful questions about those choices. It helps separate a bad result caused by a rule from a decision made because of a person’s trait, while also showing why both kinds of cases may deserve attention.

important_terms.definition: A situation in which someone is treated worse or loses an opportunity because of a trait they have.
A feature of a person, such as age, religion, sex, disability, or race.
A setback or loss, such as losing a job, a home, or a chance to join an activity.
A way of thinking about when an action is morally wrong and when it is allowed.

questions_to_think_about: Does someone have to be made worse off for discrimination to happen?
Can a rule be unfair if nobody meant to treat a group badly?
Is every choice based on a personal trait discrimination?
What might make discrimination morally wrong?

summaries.example: Suppose a company dismisses every worker shorter than 5 feet 10 inches. The rule says nothing about sex, and the manager may never think of any worker as a woman or a man. Yet because women are, on average, less likely to meet the height rule, the policy may disadvantage women more than men. On a motivational account, it may not be discrimination against women because sex was not a motivating reason. On a causal-explanatory account, it may be indirect discrimination because sex helps explain the unequal effect. Philosophers also ask whether the policy is wrong in itself or merely unjustified when its benefits do not outweigh its costs.
summaries.summary: The entry develops a philosophical framework for analyzing discrimination. Its generic definition treats discrimination as disadvantaging a person because of a trait they possess. This framework leaves several questions open. Disadvantage may be understood through comparison with others or through a counterfactual question about how the same person would have fared without the trait. It may be local, affecting one part of a person’s life, even when the person’s overall wellbeing improves. The because-of relation may be motivational: the trait appears in the agent’s reasons. Or it may be explanatory: the trait causally explains the disadvantage, including through unconscious processes or a neutral rule with unequal effects. The entry also asks which traits qualify. An unrestricted view includes arbitrary traits, while narrower views emphasize social salience or membership in historically disadvantaged groups. Another central issue is whether discrimination is a moralized concept. The generic definition can remain morally neutral, leaving a further inquiry into wrongness. Harm-based views focus on setbacks to wellbeing; disrespect views focus on failing to give people’s interests or status proper weight; expressivist views focus on demeaning social meaning; pluralist views combine multiple explanations. These debates also shape how philosophers understand indirect discrimination and its relation to law.
key_ideas: The entry separates defining discrimination from explaining why discrimination is morally wrong.
The disadvantage may be interpersonal, comparing people with one another, or counterfactual, comparing a person with how they would have fared without the trait.
A person can be locally disadvantaged in one part of life even if their overall wellbeing later improves.
Motivational and explanatory accounts of the because-of link produce different answers about implicit and indirect discrimination.
Views about traits differ: some allow any trait, while others focus on socially salient traits or traits connected with disadvantaged groups.
Leading accounts of wrongness appeal to harm, disrespect, social meaning, or a plural combination.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinctions matter because similar-looking cases can raise different moral questions. A conscious stereotype, an unconscious pattern, and a neutral rule with unequal effects may differ in explanation while still producing serious concerns. Separating moral definition from legal policy also prevents us from assuming that whatever a law prohibits, or whatever people call discriminatory, has exactly the same philosophical meaning.

important_terms.definition: A proposed general account: discrimination disadvantages a victim because of a trait the victim possesses.
The connection between a trait and a disadvantage. It may involve a person’s reasons, or a causal explanation of the outcome.
An approach saying the trait must figure in the decision-maker’s motivating reasons.
An approach saying the trait must help causally explain why the person was disadvantaged, even without conscious awareness.
Discrimination in which the decision directly uses a representation of the relevant trait.
Discrimination in which a seemingly neutral rule disadvantages people with a trait more than others.
The idea that the word discrimination can describe a case without making moral wrongness part of its definition.
The view that discrimination can be wrong for several reasons, such as harm and disrespect, rather than one reason alone.

questions_to_think_about: Should an act count as discrimination when the decision-maker has no conscious bias but the rule has unequal effects?
Is a person disadvantaged if an apparent loss leads to greater overall wellbeing later?
Should every arbitrary distinction count as discrimination, or only distinctions tied to important social patterns?
Can an act be discriminatory but morally permissible?
Are harm and disrespect separate wrong-making features, or different forms of one deeper problem?

summaries.example: A school chooses students for a team by allowing only people who can run a certain distance. The rule does not mention disability. If students with some disabilities are much more likely to be left out, philosophers might call this indirect discrimination. One question is whether the rule is discriminatory because the school meant to exclude those students. Another is whether the students’ disability helps explain why they were excluded, even if the school never thought about disability. A further question is whether the rule is justified by a real need for the team or whether it unfairly ignores the students’ interests.
summaries.summary: The entry studies discrimination as a problem in moral philosophy, while keeping it distinct from the separate question of what antidiscrimination law should do. Its starting point is a general definition: discrimination disadvantages someone because of a trait. Each part of that definition is debated. Disadvantage may be comparative, involving treatment worse than another group receives, or counterfactual, involving what would have happened if the person did not have the trait. It can be local rather than global: losing one opportunity can be a disadvantage even if a person later ends up better off overall. The phrase “because of” is also contested. A motivational view requires the trait to be among the decision-maker’s reasons. An explanatory view instead asks whether the trait helps cause or explain the disadvantage, which can include unconscious bias and neutral rules with unequal effects. Philosophers further disagree about which traits count. Some allow any arbitrary trait; others appeal to social salience or a trait’s connection with historically disadvantaged groups. The entry suggests that discrimination need not be defined as wrong from the start. Once the concept is clarified, theories of wrongness can ask whether discrimination harms wellbeing, disrespects people as equals, communicates a demeaning social meaning, or combines several wrong-making features. These choices lead to different views of indirect discrimination and of the relationship between moral philosophy and law.
key_ideas: Philosophers begin with the idea of disadvantage because of a trait, but they disagree about each part of that idea.
Disadvantage can involve comparison with other people or comparison with what the same person might have experienced in a different situation.
A person may be harmed in one area even if their total situation improves.
Some theories require a trait to motivate the decision; others allow a trait to explain an outcome without conscious intent.
Some philosophers include arbitrary traits, while others restrict discrimination to socially important or disadvantaged groups.
The moral wrongness of discrimination may involve harm, disrespect, a demeaning message, or several reasons together.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help us examine fairness without treating every unequal outcome as identical. They also show why intention alone may not settle a case: a person can lack conscious bias while following a rule that predictably disadvantages a group. At the same time, unequal effects do not automatically answer every moral question; we may still need to consider reasons, social context, harms, and competing interests.

important_terms.definition: Treating someone worse, or putting them at a disadvantage, because of a trait they have.
A feature that identifies a person, such as age, religion, sex, disability, or race.
A loss or setback compared with a relevant alternative or with how others are treated.
The link that explains why a trait and a disadvantage belong together in a case.
A rule or action that uses a trait openly or through a decision-maker’s representation of it.
A neutral-looking rule that affects people with one trait worse than people without it.
The view that a word describes a fact without itself saying whether that fact is morally wrong.
An approach holding that discrimination can be wrong because of more than one feature, such as harm and disrespect.

questions_to_think_about: If a rule has unequal effects but no one intended them, should it count as discrimination?
Can a decision be discriminatory even when it helps someone overall?
Should choosing by a random feature, such as a favorite color, count as discrimination?
Why might philosophers want to define discrimination before deciding whether it is wrong?
Which seems more important in a case: the decision-maker’s reason, the result, or the social meaning?
